newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - South African insurers grapple with AIDS.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - South African insurers grapple with AIDS.

text.p: The rapid spread of AIDS in South Africa, where abut four percent of the population is already infected, poses special problems for the life assurance industry.

The sector has reacted with a two-pronged approach. It offers policies for people who can prove they are virus-free, but also offers policies specifically designed for those testing positive -- the first of their kind in the world.
Industry experts say life assurers have to prepare long before the virus -- whose incubation period is measured in years -- starts to cause large numbers of deaths.

"It is a huge risk and will require very careful management, otherwise it is going to be disastrous for our business and our customers," said Theo Hartwig, chief actuary at South Africa's biggest life assurer, Old Mutual.
The scale of the problem in South Africa is huge.
Figures vary but about four percent of South Africa's population, or 1.5 million people, are already infected and levels will rise in the years to come.

Dealing with AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome), and its dormant HIV phase, has caused controversy as the life industry struggles with the moral issues of the epidemic while also trying to take decisions based on good business sense.
Southern Life, the country's fourth biggest life assurer, has come under heavy criticism from some quarters for its Exclusive Life policy, launched in 1993.

To qualify the holder must test negative for HIV every five years. The thinking behind it is that the creation of an HIV-free pool will shelter premiums from the inevitable rise which will accompany the increasing number of deaths from AIDS.
"That has been one of the main ways we have tried to market it," said Tom Moultrie, Southern Life deputy manager.

The policy has been a great success, contributing 30 percent of Southern Life's new business. "There are a significant number of people who, because of their lifestyle, consider themselves at low risk of infection. We are meeting that need," he added.

Analysts, too, have been impressed by Exclusive Life's performance. "Southern's sales are doing extremely well. Their sales have been very impressive, better than the competition expected," said Alan McConnochie of stockbroker BOE NatWest.
But some firms have taken the opposite path.

Earlier this year Metropolitan Life launched a policy aimed at those suffering with HIV or other serious illnesses. In a move many interpreted as a pointed dig at Southern, MetLife called its product Inclusive Life.
The move started a trend and Fedlife launched a similar product soon afterwards. Now Old Mutual is to join in with a policy industry sources say will be launched around December.
"We have to do what we can to make life better for people who are HIV positive. We don't want to turn them away from our business...it is not aimed at just generating income," Hartwig said.

But philanthropy is mixed with business sense. Spencer McNally, product development actuary at Metlife, said that on a personal level the moral aspect was paramount. But as a business there is some profit to be made.

The business of all-life assurance is about assessing the risk of mortality. With HIV-infected people the ground rules change dramatically, but the principles remain the same. "It is financially sound and it is a good business decision," he said.

Also the more business conducted with HIV sufferers the easier it becomes to build up a comprehensive database and make risk-assessment more accurate. "That can be a strong competitive advantage...we are not a charity," McNally said.

There is also a boost from creating an image as a caring firm that could attract new business to other policies. "In retrospect we believe it has definitely paid off and raised public awareness of the company," McNally said.
With these advantages in mind, Southern too may eventually start an inclusive policy. "It is not a possibility Southern Life has ruled out. It is something that has been discussed," Moultrie said.
Industry experts say the two strategies work together and simply serve their own niches. In fact Metlife and Old Mutual also run Exclusive-style policies.
AIDS campaigners say such a response is no surprise from an industry based on cool-headed judgment of life and death risks.

"They are the ultimate pragmatists. My sense is that none of this would have happened if we had not been pushing them so hard, but they are realistic people and sensitive to public pressure," said Morna Cornell, director of the AIDS Consortium.
